lessons.description: Search ads versus social ads, attribution models, and the four money formulas.
lessons.content:
## Before you use this

> **Everything on this page goes out of date.** Interfaces move, free tiers
> change, features are renamed and removed. This sheet covers what each tool is
> *for* and what to look for inside it. Check the current interface, the current
> terms and the current pricing yourself before you rely on any of it.

Ad platforms change their campaign types, their controls and their reporting
more often than almost any other category of software. Learn the concepts; look
up the buttons.

---

## The two ad platforms this course uses

```
  SEARCH ADS                        SOCIAL ADS
  someone is looking for it         someone is scrolling past it
  intent is high                    intent is low
  you buy keywords                  you buy audiences
  creative is text-first            creative is the whole job
  demand capture                    demand creation
```

That difference drives everything else. On search you are competing for someone
who already wants the thing. On social you are interrupting, so the creative has
to earn the attention first.

## Search ads: what to look for

**Structure.** Campaign holds budget and settings; ad group holds one tight
theme of keywords; ads sit inside the ad group. One theme per ad group, always.

**Match types.** Control how loosely a search can match your keyword. Looser
match reaches more and wastes more.

**Negative keywords.** The highest-value half hour in search advertising is
reading the actual search terms report and adding negatives.

**Quality signals.** Engines score the relevance of keyword, ad and landing
page. A better score generally means better placement for less. The exact
calculation is not published.

**Conversion tracking.** Set it up before you spend anything. Running ads
without conversion tracking means you will optimise towards clicks, which is not
what you want.

**The habit:** check the search terms report weekly for the first month. It
will show you things you would never have predicted.

## Social ads: what to look for

**Structure.** Campaign holds the objective; ad set holds the audience, budget
and placement; ads hold the creative.

**Audiences.** Three kinds worth knowing: audiences you upload or build from
your own data, audiences the platform builds to resemble those, and broad
targeting where the platform finds people itself.

**The pixel or tag.** A snippet on your site that reports actions back. Install
and test it before launch; a campaign optimising on a broken signal will spend
the budget cheerfully.

**Creative.** On social, creative is the targeting. Test hooks, not just images.

**The habit:** change one thing at a time, and give it long enough to mean
something. Most beginners restart campaigns before there is any data.

## Analytics

**What it answers:** where visitors came from, what they did, and which of it
led anywhere.

**The four things to set up first:**

1. Analytics installed on every page, including the thank-you page.
2. Conversions defined — the specific actions that matter.
3. UTM conventions agreed and written down.
4. A dashboard with no more than six tiles.

**The trap:** analytics tools change their data models and their report names.
When a number jumps, check whether the measurement changed before you explain
the business reason.

## Attribution, briefly

Attribution decides which touchpoint gets credit. Every model is wrong in a
different way:

| Model | Gives credit to | Hides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Last click | The final touch before converting | Everything that created the demand |
| First click | The first touch | Everything that closed it |
| Linear | All touches equally | Which one actually mattered |
| Data-driven | Whatever the platform's model decides | Its own workings |

Platforms also report on their own ads, which is a conflict of interest, not a
conspiracy. Expect the sum of platform-reported conversions to exceed the real
total.

## Spreadsheets: the four formulas

These you should be able to write from memory. Module 11 covers them properly.

```
  ROI  = (revenue - cost) / cost                 as a percentage
  ROAS = revenue from ads / ad spend             as a ratio, e.g. 3.2
  CAC  = total acquisition cost / new customers
  LTV  = average order value
         x purchases per year
         x years retained
         x gross margin
```

Two rules. **Compare LTV with CAC, never either alone** — a high CAC is fine if
LTV is far higher. And **say which costs are in CAC**: ad spend only, or ad
spend plus salaries and tools. Both are legitimate, and comparing one against
the other is not.

:::checklist Ads and analytics launch checklist
- Conversion tracking installed and a test conversion recorded
- Pixel or tag firing on the right pages
- UTM convention written down and shared
- Campaign structure has one theme or audience per ad set
- At least two ads per ad set, differing in one thing
- Negative keyword list started (search)
- Budget and end date set, so nothing runs forever unattended
- Written prediction of what will happen, to compare against
- A date in the diary to review, far enough out to have data
:::

lessons.title: Cheat sheet: email, automation and AI tools
lessons.description: Deliverability basics, the three parts of any automation, and safe use of AI tools.
lessons.content:
## Before you use this

> **Everything on this page goes out of date.** Interfaces move, free tiers
> change, features are renamed and removed. This sheet covers what each tool is
> *for* and what to look for inside it. Check the current interface, the current
> terms and the current pricing yourself before you rely on any of it.

---

## Email tools

**What they do:** hold your list, send to segments of it, automate sequences,
and report what happened.

**What to look for when choosing one:**

- Can it segment on behaviour, not just on fields you typed in?
- Can it run a sequence triggered by an action?
- Does it let you authenticate your sending domain?
- Can you export your list whenever you want?

That last one matters most. A tool you cannot leave owns your audience.

**Deliverability basics.** Getting into the inbox is mostly about proving you
are who you say you are, and sending to people who want it:

```
  AUTHENTICATE      set up the sending domain records your provider asks for
  PERMISSION        only ever email people who asked
  CLEAN             remove addresses that never open, on a schedule
  CONSISTENT        regular sending beats sudden bursts
  EASY EXIT         a clear unsubscribe link, honoured immediately
```

The exact records and their names are set by your provider and change. Follow
their current documentation.

**The habit:** before any big send, send to yourself and read it on a phone.
Most email is read on a phone and most is designed on a laptop.

## Automation tools

**What they do:** connect tools that do not know about each other. When this
happens in tool A, do that in tool B.

**The three pieces of any automation:**

```
  TRIGGER      what starts it        "a form is submitted"
  CONDITIONS   when it should run    "only if the budget field is over X"
  ACTIONS      what happens          "create a CRM record, then send an email"
```

**Webhooks.** A webhook is one system telling another that something happened,
by sending it a message. You give tool A a URL from tool B; tool A posts to it
when the event fires.

**Never put a secret in a workflow you share.** API keys and tokens belong in
the tool's credential store, referenced by name. If you export a blueprint to
share, check it carries no key.

**The habit:** every automation needs a failure path. What happens when the
other tool is down, or the data is malformed? An automation that silently drops
leads is worse than no automation.

:::checklist Automation safety checklist
- The trigger is specific enough not to fire on everything
- Conditions tested with a case that should NOT pass
- No API key, token or password typed into a step
- A failure notification goes to a human
- Tested end to end with a real record before going live
- Documented: what it does, who owns it, how to turn it off
:::

## AI tools

Covered properly in module 15. The short version for day-to-day work.

**What they are genuinely good at:** first drafts, rewriting for a different
audience, summarising long material, generating variations to choose between,
explaining something you half-understand, and getting you past a blank page.

**What they are bad at:** facts you cannot check, anything needing current data,
your brand's voice without a lot of steering, and knowing when it is wrong.

**The rule that matters:**

> Anything a model states as fact is a draft of a fact. You are the publisher,
> and you are accountable for it.

**A prompt worth reusing:**

```
  ROLE      You are writing for <audience>, who know <level of knowledge>.
  TASK      Write <what>, in <format>, of about <length>.
  CONTEXT   <the facts, pasted in - do not make the model guess them>
  STYLE     <three adjectives, plus what to avoid>
  CONSTRAIN Do not invent statistics, names or quotes. If a fact is needed
            that I have not given you, write FACT NEEDED instead of guessing.
```

That last line is the useful one. It converts invention into a visible gap.

**Never paste anything confidential** — client data, personal data, anything
under an agreement — into a tool without checking what it does with it. The
terms change; check them each time it matters.

:::checklist AI use checklist
- Every factual claim verified against a source I can point at
- No statistics quoted that I cannot attribute
- No client or personal data pasted in
- Output edited into our own voice, not published raw
- Disclosure where it is required, honest where it is not
- A human approved it before it went out
:::

## What never changes

Tools change constantly. These do not:

- Own your list. Rented audiences get taken away.
- Permission beats reach. Sending to people who want it fixes most
  deliverability problems before they start.
- Automate a process that works. Automating a broken one produces broken
  results faster.
- A model's confidence is not evidence.

lessons.title: Career roadmap and portfolio checklist
lessons.description: The six roles, a sequence that works, and exactly what belongs in a first portfolio.
lessons.content:
## The six roles

Digital marketing is not one job. Module 19 covers these in depth; this is the
map.

| Role | What they actually do all day | Strongest skills |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SEO specialist | Keyword and intent research, on-page and technical fixes, audits, content briefs | Patience, analysis, working with developers |
| Social media manager | Calendar, content, community, replies, platform analytics | Writing, visual judgement, consistency |
| Performance marketer | Builds and optimises paid campaigns, watches cost per result | Numbers, testing discipline, creative judgement |
| Content marketer | Strategy, pillars, calendar, writing and commissioning | Writing, editing, structure |
| Email marketer | Lists, sequences, segmentation, deliverability | Copywriting, systems thinking |
| Analyst | Measurement setup, dashboards, reporting, attribution | Spreadsheets, scepticism, explaining numbers |

Nobody is strong at all six. Pick one to be good at and one to be dangerous in.

## A sequence that works

```
  1  LEARN         finish the course, including the assignments
  2  PRACTISE      do the capstone properly on one brand
  3  EVIDENCE      turn the work into 3 to 5 case studies
  4  PROOF         do real work: a charity, a family business, a friend's shop
  5  VISIBILITY    one profile that says what you do, and work you can show
  6  ASK           apply, or pitch, and do it badly until you do it well
```

Most people stall between 3 and 4. The jump from course projects to real work is
the hard one, and it is almost always made by doing something small for free or
cheap, for someone who actually needed it.

## Specialist or generalist

Both work. They work differently.

**Specialist** — easier to be hired for, easier to charge for, easier to explain.
Riskier if the speciality shrinks.

**Generalist** — suits small businesses and agencies, and freelancing, where one
person does everything. Harder to stand out early.

A workable compromise: be a generalist who is visibly excellent at one thing.
The one thing gets you the conversation; the breadth keeps you useful.

## The first-portfolio problem

You need work to get work. The ways out, in order of how well they work:

1. **Do the capstone properly and present it as a case study.** Label it as a
   course project. Hirers respect clearly labelled practice work far more than
   vague claims.
2. **Do real work for a small organisation.** A local charity, a family
   business, a society. Small scope, real constraints, a real result.
3. **Audit a real business and send the audit.** Unrequested, free, genuinely
   useful. It demonstrates the skill directly and sometimes wins the client.
4. **Document your own project.** A niche site, a channel, a newsletter. It
   proves you can do it without anyone's permission.

Never present a course project as a paid client engagement. It is checkable, and
being caught ends the conversation.

## What goes in a portfolio

Three to five pieces, each one a case study rather than a screenshot.

:::checklist Portfolio checklist
THE BASICS
- A one-line description of what I do and who for
- A way to contact me that works
- Three to five case studies, not twenty
- Each case study labelled: real client, or course project

EACH CASE STUDY CONTAINS
- The situation: what the business needed
- What was in the way
- What I did, and why that approach
- What I deliberately did not do
- The result, and how it was measured
- What I would do differently
- Evidence: screenshots, files or links
- Permission to show it, if it is real client work

THE WORK ITSELF
- At least one piece showing strategy, not just execution
- At least one piece with a number in it that I can explain
- At least one piece in my chosen speciality
- Nothing that quotes a result I cannot stand behind

PROFILE
- Headline says what I do, not what I am looking for
- The work is visible without anyone having to ask for it
- A short note on what kind of problem I like working on

HONESTY
- No invented client names
- No invented metrics
- No implied employment at a company I did not work for
- Course projects named as course projects
:::

## Freelancing: the first six months

Module 19 covers proposals, pricing and client communication properly. The
things people most often get wrong:

**Pricing by the hour forever.** Hourly pricing punishes you for getting faster.
Move to project or retainer pricing once you can estimate reliably.

**Saying yes to everything.** The worst clients arrive first, because
experienced buyers already have someone. Learn to turn work down.

**No written scope.** Almost every freelancing disaster is a scope disaster.
Write down what is included, what is not, and how changes get priced — template
28 and the contract outline in template 29.

**Promising results.** Never promise a ranking, a revenue figure or a growth
rate. Promise the work, the process and the reporting. Clients who demand
guarantees have usually been let down by someone who gave them.

**Not reporting.** Clients churn when they cannot see what they are paying for,
even when the work is good. A short monthly report is retention.

## What this course does and does not give you

**It gives you:** the concepts, a worked practice of each one, a portfolio of
assignments, a capstone you can present, and five completion certificates from
this platform.

**It does not give you:** a job, a vendor certification, or any guarantee about
income or results. Those depend on your market, your effort and a certain amount
of luck. Anyone telling you otherwise is selling something.

The people who get work from a course like this are, almost without exception,
the ones who did the assignments properly and then did something real for
someone.

lessons.title: Level 1 exam: Digital Marketing Beginner
lessons.description: Modules 1 to 5. Twenty questions plus two applied tasks, marked out of 40, pass 24.
lessons.content:
## How this exam works

**Marked out of 40. Pass mark 24.**

- Twenty multiple-choice questions, one mark each, checked in your browser.
- Two applied tasks, ten marks each, which you mark yourself against the guide
  at the bottom of the page.

Nothing is recorded. The honesty of your own marking is the whole value: a
score you inflated tells you nothing.

Sit this with your notes closed. If you score below 24, the answer key tells you
which module to go back to.

**Covers modules 1 to 5:** fundamentals, websites and landing pages, SEO,
content marketing and social media.

---

## Part A: twenty multiple-choice questions

:::quiz
Q. A business has strong traffic and almost no enquiries. Which job is failing?
- Get found
+ Get chosen
- Get kept
- None, this is normal
= Traffic proves "get found" works. The failure is persuasion, which happens on the destination.

Q. Which is the best description of owned media?
+ Channels you control, which nobody can take away from you
- Channels where you do not pay per click
- Channels that produce the most traffic
- Channels where competitors cannot advertise
= Control and permanence define it, not cost. Your site, your email list, your messaging list.

Q. At which funnel stage does a comparison guide fit best?
- Awareness
+ Consideration
- Retention
- Advocacy
= A comparison helps someone already weighing you against alternatives.

Q. A B2B purchase stalls after the user is enthusiastic. The most useful next step is to:
+ Give them something they can forward to the budget holder
- Offer a time-limited discount
- Call the user more often
- Rebuild the product demonstration
= B2B decisions involve several people, and the user usually cannot sign.

Q. What is the single job of a landing page?
+ To get one specific action from one specific audience
- To explain everything the business offers
- To rank for as many keywords as possible
- To look better than competitors' pages
= Breadth belongs on a website. A landing page is built around one conversion.

Q. Why should a paid ad usually not point at the home page?
+ The ad made a specific promise and the home page does not keep it
- Home pages load more slowly than other pages
- Ad platforms penalise home-page destinations
- Home pages cannot be tracked
= Continuity between the ad and the destination is what converts.

Q. Which change is most likely to improve a lead form's completion rate?
+ Removing fields that are not needed yet
- Adding a field asking how they found you
- Making the submit button a different colour
- Moving the form lower down the page
= Every extra field is friction. Ask for what you need to take the next step, nothing more.

Q. What does a call to action need to be effective?
+ Specific about what happens next
- Written in capital letters
- Repeated at least five times
- Placed only at the bottom of the page
= "Get the free checklist" tells the visitor what they get. "Submit" tells them nothing.

Q. A page is crawled but never appears in results. What has not happened?
+ Indexing
- Crawling
- Ranking
- Rendering
= Crawling fetches the page; indexing stores it so it can be returned. Ranking comes after.

Q. Which best describes search intent?
+ What the searcher actually wants from the query they typed
- How many people search for a term each month
- How difficult a keyword is to rank for
- Which search engine someone used
= Intent decides what kind of page can satisfy the query at all.

Q. Two pages on a site target the same keyword. What should usually happen?
+ Merge them into one stronger page
- Leave both, to double the chances
- Delete the older one without redirecting
- Add the keyword to both titles more often
= Two pages competing for one query split the signals and usually both underperform.

Q. What is the purpose of internal linking?
+ To pass relevance between your own pages and help both users and crawlers find them
- To increase the total number of links pointing at the site
- To reduce page load time
- To replace the need for a sitemap
= Internal links guide people and crawlers towards the pages that matter.

Q. Which of these is on-page SEO rather than technical SEO?
+ Writing a unique title tag for the page
- Fixing a redirect chain
- Submitting a sitemap
- Improving server response time
= On-page is work on the content and its markup; technical is how the site is built and served.

Q. What is a content pillar?
+ One of a few themes every piece of content ties back to
- A long article that supports several shorter ones
- A platform the brand publishes on
- The main heading of a blog post
= Pillars keep a calendar coherent so the brand becomes known for a few things.

Q. What is the main purpose of a lead magnet?
+ To exchange something genuinely useful for permission to make contact
- To improve search rankings
- To fill the content calendar
- To reduce advertising costs
= It converts an anonymous reader into a contactable lead.

Q. Content repurposing means:
+ Turning one piece of work into several formats for different channels
- Publishing the same post on every platform unchanged
- Updating old posts with the current date
- Buying content from a writer and rebranding it
= The idea is reused; the format changes to suit each channel.

Q. Why does a content calendar usually fail?
+ More is planned than anyone has time to produce
- It is not detailed enough
- It covers too few platforms
- It is not shared with the audience
= An ambitious calendar nobody can deliver produces guilt, not content.

Q. When choosing social platforms, the deciding question is:
+ Where does our audience already spend attention on this kind of problem
- Which platform is growing fastest
- Which platform the team enjoys using
- Which platform competitors post on most
= The audience's existing habits decide the channel. Everything else is a guess.

Q. What does an engagement rate tell you that follower count does not?
+ Whether the audience actually responds to anything
- How many people could possibly see a post
- How much the account cost to grow
- Whether the account is run professionally
= A large indifferent audience is worth less than a small responsive one.

Q. A brand posts identical content to LinkedIn and Instagram and performance is poor on both. The most likely reason is:
+ The format and tone each platform rewards are different
- The posting times were wrong
- The hashtags were wrong
- The content was too long
= Same idea, different execution. One format rarely fits two audiences in two contexts.
:::

---

## Part B: two applied tasks

**Task 1 (10 marks).** Choose one of the four fictional brands from this course.
Write a landing page plan on one page: the single audience, the single action,
the headline, three proof points, the form fields you would ask for and why, and
the one thing you would test first.

**Task 2 (10 marks).** For the same brand, write five keywords with the search
intent of each, say which single page would target each keyword, and name one
keyword you deliberately rejected and why.

## How to mark the applied tasks

Mark yourself hard. For each task, award marks only where the evidence is
actually on your page.

A good habit: leave the task for a day, then mark it as if a stranger wrote it.
Everyone marks their own work generously on the day they wrote it.

### Task 1 marking guide

| What earns marks | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| One audience named specifically, not "everyone interested" | 2 |
| One action, and only one | 2 |
| Headline states a benefit to that audience rather than describing the product | 2 |
| Three proof points that are checkable, not adjectives | 2 |
| Form fields justified, with at least one field deliberately left out | 1 |
| A test named, with what you expect to happen | 1 |

### Task 2 marking guide

| What earns marks | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| Five keywords that a real person would plausibly type | 2 |
| Intent correctly labelled for each | 3 |
| One page per keyword, with no two keywords sharing a page | 2 |
| The rejected keyword, with a reason about intent or fit rather than volume | 3 |

### If you scored below 24

| You got these wrong | Go back to |
| --- | --- |
| Questions 1 to 4 | Module 1 |
| Questions 5 to 8 | Module 2 |
| Questions 9 to 13 | Module 3 |
| Questions 14 to 17 | Module 4 |
| Questions 18 to 20 | Module 5 |

Re-read the module, redo its lab, then sit this again in a few days rather than
immediately.

lessons.title: Level 2 exam: Digital Marketing Intermediate
lessons.description: Modules 6 to 12. Twenty questions plus two applied tasks, marked out of 40, pass 24.
lessons.content:
## How this exam works

**Marked out of 40. Pass mark 24.**

- Twenty multiple-choice questions, one mark each, checked in your browser.
- Two applied tasks, ten marks each, which you mark yourself against the guide
  at the bottom of the page.

Nothing is recorded. The honesty of your own marking is the whole value: a
score you inflated tells you nothing.

Sit this with your notes closed. If you score below 24, the answer key tells you
which module to go back to.

**Covers modules 6 to 12:** social advertising, Google Ads, YouTube, email,
WhatsApp and conversational marketing, analytics, and conversion rate
optimisation.

---

## Part A: twenty multiple-choice questions

:::quiz
Q. In a social ads account, what belongs at the ad set level rather than the campaign level?
+ The audience and the budget for that audience
- The overall objective
- The payment method
- The business account settings
= Campaign holds the objective; ad set holds audience, budget and placement; ads hold creative.

Q. What is a custom audience built from?
+ Your own data, such as a customer list or site visitors
- People the platform thinks resemble your customers
- Everyone who has seen your ad
- A demographic selection you type in
= Custom audiences use data you supply. Lookalikes are what the platform builds from them.

Q. A pixel is installed but fires on every page as a purchase. What is the consequence?
+ The campaign optimises towards the wrong action and wastes budget confidently
- The pixel will be disabled automatically
- Nothing, as long as the conversion count looks high
- Only reporting is affected, not delivery
= Optimisation follows the signal it is given. A wrong signal is worse than none.

Q. On search, what does a negative keyword do?
+ Prevents the ad from showing when that term appears in the search
- Lowers the bid for that term
- Removes the term from your keyword list
- Reports the term as irrelevant to the platform
= Negatives exclude traffic that will never convert, so budget goes to intent.

Q. Why does one theme per ad group matter?
+ Mixed themes make the ad less relevant to each search and the results unreadable
- Platforms limit the number of keywords per ad group
- It reduces the cost per click automatically
- It is required for conversion tracking
= Tight grouping lets the ad match the search, which is what relevance scoring rewards.

Q. Which best describes the role of a quality or relevance score in search advertising?
+ An estimate of how relevant keyword, ad and landing page are, which affects placement and cost
- A measure of how much you are willing to bid
- A ranking of your account against competitors
- A score for how well the website is designed
= Relevance can get better placement for less money. The exact calculation is not published.

Q. Someone searches a broad category term and your ad appears via a loose match type. What is the main risk?
+ You pay for clicks from people wanting something you do not sell
- The ad will be rejected
- Your Quality Score cannot be calculated
- The search engine will stop showing your ads
= Looser matching reaches more people and wastes more budget without negatives.

Q. On YouTube, what is the thumbnail's job?
+ To earn the click against everything else on the screen
- To summarise the video's content accurately
- To include the title text again
- To match the channel's colour scheme
= Title and thumbnail compete for attention first. Nothing else matters if nobody clicks.

Q. What does video SEO mainly affect?
+ Whether the video is found by people searching, on the platform and off it
- How long people watch once they start
- The video's production quality
- Whether the video can be monetised
= Discovery is the job. Retention is a separate problem handled by the content.

Q. A channel's videos get many impressions and very few views. What should be examined first?
+ Titles and thumbnails
- Video length
- Upload schedule
- Description keywords
= Impressions mean it was offered to people who then did not click.

Q. Why is an email list described as owned media?
+ You can reach those people without a platform deciding who sees it
- Email costs nothing to send
- Email cannot be blocked
- Lists cannot be bought or sold
= Ownership is about control of access to the audience, not cost.

Q. What is the main job of the first email in a welcome sequence?
+ Deliver what was promised and set expectations for what comes next
- Make the first sale
- Ask for a review
- Introduce the whole product range
= Keeping the promise immediately is what earns the right to send the rest.

Q. Which practice most protects email deliverability?
+ Removing contacts who have not engaged for a long time
- Sending more often so the list stays warm
- Using more images and less text
- Avoiding unsubscribe links
= Sending to people who do not engage teaches providers that your mail is unwanted. Removing an unsubscribe link is also generally unlawful.

Q. A campaign shows a high open rate and almost no clicks. What is the most likely explanation?
+ The subject line promised something the email did not deliver
- The list is too small
- The send time was wrong
- The emails landed in spam
= Opens prove the subject worked. The gap is between the promise and the content.

Q. What distinguishes conversational marketing from email marketing?
+ It is a two-way thread where the customer expects a quick reply
- It is cheaper per message
- It cannot be automated
- It reaches more people per send
= The medium sets the expectation. A chat implies a conversation, not a broadcast.

Q. What is the most common way businesses damage a messaging channel?
+ Treating it as a broadcast channel and sending too often
- Replying too quickly
- Using automation at all
- Asking questions in the first message
= Messaging apps are personal space. Overuse gets you muted or reported faster than email.

Q. What does a UTM parameter do?
+ Tags a link so analytics can attribute the visit to a source, medium and campaign
- Shortens a long URL
- Prevents a link from being indexed
- Redirects a visitor to a tracking page first
= UTMs are how a click is attributed. They change nothing about the destination.

Q. Why does inconsistent UTM capitalisation cause problems?
+ Analytics treats differently-cased values as separate sources, splitting the data
- The links stop working
- Search engines penalise it
- The platform rejects the link
= Agree a convention once, write it down, and keep to it.

Q. Which pair gives the most useful picture together?
+ CAC and LTV
- CAC and impressions
- ROAS and bounce rate
- LTV and click-through rate
= A high acquisition cost is fine when lifetime value is far higher. Either number alone misleads.

Q. In a conversion test, five changes are made at once and the rate improves. What have you learned?
+ That something helped, but not what, so you cannot repeat it deliberately
- Which change was responsible
- That all five changes were good
- Nothing at all
= A test isolates one variable. Bundled changes give a result you cannot act on.
:::

---

## Part B: two applied tasks

**Task 1 (10 marks).** For a fictional brand of your choice, write a campaign
structure for one paid channel: the objective, two ad sets or ad groups with
their audiences or keyword themes, two ads each with their hooks, the conversion
event you would track, and your written prediction of what will happen.

**Task 2 (10 marks).** Design a five-email welcome sequence for the same brand.
For each email give the send timing, the subject line, the single job of that
email, and the one link in it. Then name the metric you would judge the whole
sequence on, and why that one.

## How to mark the applied tasks

Mark yourself hard. For each task, award marks only where the evidence is
actually on your page.

A good habit: leave the task for a day, then mark it as if a stranger wrote it.
Everyone marks their own work generously on the day they wrote it.

### Task 1 marking guide

| What earns marks | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| Objective matches what the business actually needs | 1 |
| Two ad sets or groups, each with a single coherent theme or audience | 3 |
| Two ads per set that differ in one deliberate way | 2 |
| A specific conversion event named, not "sales" | 2 |
| A written prediction, with a number in it | 2 |

### Task 2 marking guide

| What earns marks | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| Five emails with sensible, stated timing | 2 |
| Each email has one job, and the jobs do not overlap | 3 |
| Email 1 delivers what was promised at sign-up | 1 |
| One link per email | 2 |
| A judging metric chosen, with a reason tied to the business objective | 2 |

### If you scored below 24

| You got these wrong | Go back to |
| --- | --- |
| Questions 1 to 3 | Module 6 |
| Questions 4 to 7 | Module 7 |
| Questions 8 to 10 | Module 8 |
| Questions 11 to 14 | Module 9 |
| Questions 15 and 16 | Module 10 |
| Questions 17 to 19 | Module 11 |
| Question 20 | Module 12 |

lessons.title: Level 3 exam: Digital Marketing Advanced
lessons.description: Modules 13 to 18. Twenty questions plus two applied tasks, marked out of 40, pass 24.
lessons.content:
## How this exam works

**Marked out of 40. Pass mark 24.**

- Twenty multiple-choice questions, one mark each, checked in your browser.
- Two applied tasks, ten marks each, which you mark yourself against the guide
  at the bottom of the page.

Nothing is recorded. Sit it with your notes closed.

**Covers modules 13 to 18:** influencer and affiliate marketing, e-commerce, AI
in marketing, AEO and GEO, marketing automation, and advanced strategy.

---

## Part A: twenty multiple-choice questions

:::quiz
Q. Why is follower count a weak basis for selecting an influencer?
+ It says nothing about whether the audience is yours or whether it acts
- Large accounts charge more than they are worth
- Follower counts cannot be verified
- Small accounts always perform better
= Relevance and engagement predict results. Reach alone does not.

Q. What is the clearest sign an influencer partnership is working?
+ Movement in the tracked action you agreed before it started
- A rise in the creator's follower count
- A high number of comments on the post
- The brand being tagged more often
= Agree the measurable action in advance, or you will be left arguing about impressions.

Q. In an affiliate programme, what does the commission model determine?
+ What behaviour you are paying for, and therefore what partners will optimise towards
- How many affiliates will join
- Which network you must use
- Whether the programme is profitable
= Pay per sale and you get sales focus; pay per lead and you get lead volume, including poor leads.

Q. On an e-commerce product page, which usually matters most to a first-time buyer?
+ Evidence that removes a specific doubt they already have
- The number of products in the range
- The brand's founding story
- A countdown timer
= Product pages convert by answering the objection, not by adding pressure.

Q. What does an abandoned cart indicate?
+ High intent that stopped short of payment
- A pricing problem
- A product nobody wants
- A broken checkout
= It may be any of those, but the signal itself is intent that did not complete.

Q. Why does customer retention matter more in e-commerce than first purchases alone suggest?
+ The hardest step, establishing trust, is already done for a returning buyer
- Returning customers always spend more per order
- Retention improves search rankings
- It reduces the need for product photography
= Winning back an existing customer is usually far easier than finding a new one.

Q. A model produces a product claim you cannot find a source for. What should you do?
+ Remove it or verify it before anything is published
- Publish it and correct it later if challenged
- Reword it so it sounds less specific
- Attribute it to the model
= Generated text states things confidently that are not true. The publisher is accountable.

Q. Which task is generative AI genuinely well suited to?
+ Producing several variations of a draft for a human to choose between
- Supplying current statistics
- Deciding the brand's positioning
- Verifying whether a claim is true
= It is a drafting and variation tool. Facts and judgement remain yours.

Q. What makes a prompt more reliable?
+ Supplying the facts in the prompt rather than expecting the model to know them
- Making the prompt as short as possible
- Asking the model to be confident
- Repeating the instruction several times
= Giving context removes the need for the model to invent it.

Q. What is the main risk of pasting client material into an AI tool?
+ You may be disclosing confidential or personal data outside an agreement
- The output will be lower quality
- The tool will refuse the request
- It slows the tool down
= Check what the tool does with input, every time it matters. Terms change.

Q. What distinguishes AEO from classic SEO?
+ The goal is being used as the answer, not only appearing in a list of links
- It only applies to voice search
- It replaces the need for technical SEO
- It is about paying for placement in AI results
= Answer Engine Optimisation targets extraction and citation inside an answer.

Q. Why does structured, well-organised content help with AI answers?
+ Clear structure makes a passage easier to extract and cite accurately
- It increases the word count
- It guarantees a citation
- It prevents competitors being cited
= Nothing guarantees a citation. Structure improves the odds of being usable.

Q. What is an entity, in the context of search?
+ A distinct thing a search engine understands, such as a person, place or brand
- A keyword with high search volume
- A page marked up with schema
- A company that owns a website
= Entities and their relationships are how knowledge graphs represent meaning.

Q. Why do brand mentions without links still matter for AI search visibility?
+ Being named consistently across sources helps engines associate you with a topic
- They pass ranking credit like links
- They can be bought more cheaply than links
- They prevent competitors ranking
= Association and consistency matter, not just hyperlinks.

Q. What are the three parts of any automation?
+ Trigger, conditions, actions
- Audience, budget, creative
- Source, medium, campaign
- Awareness, consideration, conversion
= Something starts it, something decides whether it should run, something happens.

Q. What does lead scoring do?
+ Ranks leads by likelihood to buy, so effort goes where it pays
- Measures customer satisfaction
- Prices a lead for resale
- Scores the quality of a landing page
= It is a prioritisation tool for finite sales attention.

Q. Where should an API key used by an automation live?
+ In the tool's credential store, referenced by name
- In the workflow step, so it is easy to find
- In a shared document the team can access
- In the webhook URL
= A key typed into a step travels with any exported or shared blueprint.

Q. What happens when you automate a process that does not work?
+ You get the broken result faster and more consistently
- The automation will fail and alert you
- The process improves because it becomes consistent
- Nothing, until volume increases
= Automation amplifies whatever it is given. Fix the process first.

Q. In STP, what does positioning establish?
+ What you stand for to a chosen audience, and how you differ from alternatives
- Which channels you will use
- How your prices compare with competitors
- Where your offices are located
= Positioning is about the place you occupy in a customer's mind.

Q. A strategy document approves every available channel. What is wrong with it?
+ It has made no decisions, so it is a wish list rather than a strategy
- It is too expensive to execute
- It will confuse the design team
- Nothing, provided the budget allows it
= The value of a strategy is in what it declines.
:::

---

## Part B: two applied tasks

**Task 1 (10 marks).** For a fictional brand, write an automation blueprint: the
trigger, at least two conditions, the sequence of actions, where credentials
live, what happens when a step fails, and who is notified.

**Task 2 (10 marks).** Write a positioning statement for the same brand using
the template from module 18, then name three channels you would use and one you
would deliberately rule out, with a reason for each.

## How to mark the applied tasks

### Task 1 marking guide

| What earns marks | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| A specific trigger that will not fire on everything | 2 |
| At least two conditions, including one that excludes a case | 2 |
| Actions in a sensible order, each one doing a single thing | 2 |
| Credentials referenced, never written into a step | 2 |
| A failure path, and a human who gets told | 2 |

### Task 2 marking guide

| What earns marks | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| Positioning statement complete, with a named main alternative | 3 |
| A competitor could not say the identical sentence | 2 |
| Three channels, each with a reason tied to the audience's existing habits | 3 |
| One channel ruled out, with a real reason rather than "no budget" | 2 |

### If you scored below 24

| You got these wrong | Go back to |
| --- | --- |
| Questions 1 to 3 | Module 13 |
| Questions 4 to 6 | Module 14 |
| Questions 7 to 10 | Module 15 |
| Questions 11 to 14 | Module 16 |
| Questions 15 to 18 | Module 17 |
| Questions 19 and 20 | Module 18 |

lessons.title: Level 4 exam: Digital Marketing Professional
lessons.description: Module 19. Twenty questions plus two applied tasks, marked out of 40, pass 24.
lessons.content:
## How this exam works

**Marked out of 40. Pass mark 24.**

- Twenty multiple-choice questions, one mark each, checked in your browser.
- Two applied tasks, ten marks each, which you mark yourself against the guide
  at the bottom of the page.

Nothing is recorded. Sit it with your notes closed.

**Covers module 19:** career paths, the six roles, freelancing, finding clients,
proposals, pricing, client communication, reporting, portfolio and professional
branding.

This level is about the business of doing the work, not the work itself.

---

## Part A: twenty multiple-choice questions

:::quiz
Q. Which role spends most of its time on measurement setup and reporting rather than campaigns?
+ Digital marketing analyst
- Performance marketer
- Content marketer
- Social media manager
= The analyst owns tracking, dashboards and the honest explanation of what the numbers mean.

Q. A performance marketer's day is mostly spent on:
+ Building and adjusting paid campaigns against a cost-per-result target
- Writing long-form articles
- Managing community replies
- Designing the website
= The job is buying results efficiently and knowing when to stop.

Q. What is the strongest argument for specialising early?
+ It is easier to be hired for, and easier to explain what you do
- Specialists always earn more
- Generalist roles are disappearing
- It requires less study
= A clear speciality gets the conversation. Breadth keeps you useful once you are in.

Q. For a first client, which usually matters most?
+ Work they can look at and judge for themselves
- The number of certificates you hold
- The length of your course
- A low price
= Evidence beats claims. A certificate supports a portfolio; it does not replace one.

Q. What is the safest way to present course projects in a portfolio?
+ Include them, clearly labelled as course projects
- Leave them out entirely
- Present them as client work since the skills are the same
- Mention them only if asked
= Clearly labelled practice work is respected. Misrepresenting it is checkable and fatal.

Q. Which is the most useful first piece of real-world experience?
+ A small, real project for an organisation that actually needed it
- A large speculative redesign of a famous brand
- A certification from a vendor
- A longer version of a course project
= Real constraints and a real result teach what no exercise can.

Q. What is the main problem with pricing by the hour indefinitely?
+ It penalises you for becoming faster at the work
- Clients dislike hourly rates
- It is difficult to invoice
- It is not legal in most places
= As you get better the same result takes less time, so hourly pricing cuts your income.

Q. Before quoting on a project, the most important thing to establish is:
+ What the client actually needs and what success looks like to them
- Which tools they currently use
- Their budget ceiling
- How quickly they can pay
= A quote for the wrong problem is wrong at any price.

Q. What belongs in the scope section of a proposal?
+ What is included, what is excluded, and how changes are priced
- A list of every tool you own
- Testimonials from other clients
- Your full CV
= Almost every freelancing dispute is a scope dispute.

Q. A client asks you to guarantee a first-page ranking. The right response is:
+ Explain that nobody can guarantee it, and offer to commit to the work and the reporting instead
- Agree, since rankings usually improve anyway
- Agree, with a long enough timeline to be safe
- Decline the conversation
= Promising a result outside your control is dishonest and usually ends badly.

Q. What is the most common cause of a client relationship ending even when the work is good?
+ The client cannot see what they are paying for
- The price was too high
- The work took too long
- The reports were too detailed
= Visibility is retention. A short regular report prevents most churn.

Q. A monthly client report should lead with:
+ A one-sentence summary of what happened and what you will do next
- A full table of every metric available
- A list of tasks completed
- The invoice
= Clients read the first line. Make it the thing they need to know.

Q. A campaign underperformed this month. The best way to report it is:
+ State it plainly, explain the likely cause, and say what changes next
- Emphasise the metrics that did improve
- Delay the report until results recover
- Attribute it to factors outside your control
= Honest reporting with a next step builds trust. Selective reporting destroys it when discovered.

Q. What makes a case study stronger than a screenshot?
+ It shows the reasoning: the situation, the decision and the result
- It is longer
- It includes the client's logo
- It contains more numbers
= Hirers are buying judgement. A screenshot shows output, not thinking.

Q. How many portfolio pieces are usually enough?
+ Three to five, each one properly explained
- As many as possible
- One, if it is excellent
- Twelve, to cover every service
= Depth beats volume. Nobody reads twenty.

Q. A professional profile headline works best when it:
+ Says what you do and for whom
- States that you are seeking opportunities
- Lists every skill you have
- Contains your job title only
= The reader is deciding in two seconds whether you solve their problem.

Q. What should you do when a prospective client's project is outside your skills?
+ Say so, and refer them on if you can
- Take it and learn on the job without telling them
- Take it and subcontract silently
- Quote high so they decline
= Turning work down honestly is the cheapest reputation you will ever buy.

Q. Which is the best reason to turn down a client?
+ The scope cannot be defined and they will not discuss it
- They are a small business
- They have worked with a freelancer before
- They asked for a detailed proposal
= Undefined scope is the single strongest predictor of a bad engagement.

Q. What is the main purpose of a written contract for a small freelance project?
+ To settle in advance what happens when something goes wrong
- To impress the client
- To satisfy tax requirements
- To prevent the client cancelling
= Contracts earn their keep when there is a disagreement, not when everything goes well.

Q. Who should own the intellectual property in work you produce for a client?
+ Whatever the contract says, commonly transferring on full payment
- The freelancer, always
- The client, always, from the moment work begins
- Neither party until the project is finished
= It is a negotiated term. The important thing is that it is written down, with your portfolio rights.
:::

---

## Part B: two applied tasks

**Task 1 (10 marks).** Write a one-page proposal for a fictional brand using
template 28: what you understand, what you propose, what they get, what you need
from them, scope, timeline, and what you do not promise.

**Task 2 (10 marks).** Write one portfolio case study using template 30, based on
a module assignment you have actually done. Label it clearly as a course
project.

## How to mark the applied tasks

### Task 1 marking guide

| What earns marks | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| The situation restated in the client's terms, not marketing jargon | 2 |
| Deliverables listed specifically enough to be checked off | 2 |
| Exclusions stated, and a method for pricing changes | 2 |
| What you need from the client, including who decides | 1 |
| A timeline with a first deliverable date | 1 |
| An explicit statement that results are not guaranteed | 2 |

### Task 2 marking guide

| What earns marks | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| Clearly labelled as a course project | 2 |
| Situation and obstacle described concretely | 2 |
| The approach explained, including one thing you chose not to do | 2 |
| Result stated with how it was measured, or honestly marked as unmeasured | 2 |
| What you would do differently | 1 |
| No invented client, metric or outcome anywhere | 1 |

Deduct all 10 marks for any invented metric or implied real client. That is the
one error this level exists to prevent.

lessons.title: Level 5 capstone: brief, rubric and presentation guide
lessons.description: The capstone brief, its sixteen deliverables, the 100-mark rubric and the presentation guide.
lessons.content:
## What Level 5 is

Levels 1 to 4 are exams. **Level 5 is the project.** There is no written exam,
because you cannot test whether someone can run a campaign by asking them
twenty questions about it.

You take one brand through everything in this course and present the result.
This is the piece of work you show an employer or a first client.

**Before you start:** finish modules 1 to 19, including the assignments. The
capstone reuses them. Starting early means producing the early deliverables
twice.

Most people spend two to four weeks on it.

---

## The brief

Choose **one** brand and take it through a full quarter of marketing, on paper.

| Brand | What it is | Best if you want to practise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Petal & Pine | D2C skincare, online only | E-commerce, paid social, retention |
| Bright Mile Dental | A single-location dental clinic | Local SEO, search ads, conversational |
| Shiftly | B2B shift-scheduling software | B2B content, long sales cycles, automation |
| Craftwise Academy | An online course seller | SEO, content, email, YouTube |
| Your own | A real small business, with permission | Everything, with real constraints |

If you use a real business, **use only what you can observe**, and label every
assumption. Do not invent figures for a real company. Where you need numbers for
a budget or forecast, state them as assumptions and show the arithmetic.

### The sixteen deliverables

Each one is a lesson in module 20. Produce all sixteen.

| # | Deliverable | What good looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Market research | Observable facts about the market, with sources, and assumptions labelled |
| 2 | Buyer persona | Situation, goal, barriers, where they look, and a "so what" |
| 3 | Competitor analysis | Three competitors, what you would do differently, and the gap nobody fills |
| 4 | Website or landing page | One audience, one action, a headline, proof and a form |
| 5 | Keyword research | Keywords with intent, one page each, and one rejected keyword |
| 6 | SEO strategy | On-page, technical and content priorities in order, with reasons |
| 7 | Content strategy | Three or four pillars, each with a reason the audience cares |
| 8 | Social media calendar | 30 days, every row tied to a pillar and carrying a CTA |
| 9 | Meta Ads campaign | Objective, structure, audiences, creative concepts, tracking |
| 10 | Google Ads campaign | Campaign type, ad groups, match types, negatives, assets |
| 11 | Email campaign | A sequence with one job and one link per email |
| 12 | Analytics setup | Conversions defined, UTM convention, what is tracked where |
| 13 | Marketing dashboard | Six tiles or fewer, each compared against a target or a prior period |
| 14 | Campaign budget | Allocation across channels, with the reasoning for the split |
| 15 | KPI and ROI report | The numbers, what moved, what you cannot explain, what changes |
| 16 | Final presentation | Ten to fifteen minutes, in the structure below |

### What to submit

One folder or document containing all sixteen, plus a one-page summary at the
front. The summary should let a reader understand your whole plan without
opening anything else.

---

## The marking rubric

**Marked out of 100. A pass is 50. A distinction is 85.**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns full marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Research and audience | 15 | Persona built from observable evidence; assumptions labelled; competitor analysis identifies a real gap |
| Strategy and positioning | 15 | A clear chain from objective to channels; a positioning statement a competitor could not copy; something deliberately ruled out |
| Organic execution | 15 | SEO and content work that targets intent, with one page per keyword and pillars the audience cares about |
| Paid execution | 15 | Both campaigns structured correctly, with tracking defined before spend and a written prediction |
| Email and retention | 10 | A sequence where each email has one job; a retention plan, not only acquisition |
| Measurement | 15 | Conversions defined, UTM convention stated, dashboard limited and comparative, KPIs leading and lagging |
| Budget and ROI | 10 | An allocation with reasoning; arithmetic that multiplies out; honest about what is assumed |
| Presentation | 5 | Clear, within time, and answers questions without defensiveness |

### Automatic deductions

| What | Deduction |
| --- | --- |
| Any invented statistic about a real company | Research and audience scores zero |
| A promised ranking, income or growth figure | −10 marks |
| Deliverables missing | −5 marks each |
| Numbers that do not multiply out, uncorrected | −10 marks |
| A fictional brand presented as a real client | Fail |

### Grade bands

| Marks | Band | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 85–100 | Distinction | Could be presented to a real client with minor edits |
| 70–84 | Strong pass | Sound throughout; one or two areas thin |
| 50–69 | Pass | The chain holds but several deliverables are generic |
| Below 50 | Resubmit | A collection of tactics rather than a campaign |

---

## The presentation guide

Ten to fifteen minutes. Assume your audience knows marketing and does not know
your brand.

### Structure

```
  1  THE SITUATION        1 min    who the brand is, what it needs, the number
  2  THE AUDIENCE         2 min    the persona, and the evidence behind it
  3  THE INSIGHT          1 min    the one thing you noticed that shaped everything
  4  THE STRATEGY         2 min    positioning, channels chosen, channels refused
  5  THE WORK             4 min    the deliverables, fast - show, do not read
  6  THE MEASUREMENT      2 min    what you would track and what would make you stop
  7  WHAT I GOT WRONG     1 min    the weakest part of your own plan
  8  QUESTIONS            2 min
```

Slide 7 is the one that distinguishes a good presentation. Everyone presents
their plan as though it is finished. Naming its weakest point tells the audience
you can be trusted with a real budget.

### Rules that save presentations

- **One idea per slide.** If you need to say "as you can see here", the slide is
  too busy.
- **Show the artefact, do not read it.** Put the calendar on screen and talk
  about why it looks like that.
- **Lead with the decision, then the evidence.** "We are not using short-form
  video, because our buyer researches before buying" beats five slides building
  to it.
- **Rehearse to time, out loud, once.** Everything takes longer than it reads.
- **Have the arithmetic ready.** The first question is almost always about the
  budget or the forecast.

### Questions you should expect

| Question | What they are really asking |
| --- | --- |
| Why that channel? | Did you choose, or did you default? |
| Where did that number come from? | Is this evidence or invention? |
| What would you do with half the budget? | Do you know what matters most? |
| What happens if it does not work? | Have you thought past the plan? |
| Why not the obvious channel? | Can you defend a deliberate omission? |

:::checklist Capstone submission checklist
- All sixteen deliverables present
- A one-page summary at the front
- Brand named, and labelled fictional or real
- Every assumption labelled as an assumption
- No invented data about any real company
- No promised ranking, income or result anywhere
- Budget arithmetic checked: the numbers multiply out
- Every KPI has a target and a reason
- At least one channel deliberately ruled out, with a reason
- At least one thing I would do differently, written down
- Presentation rehearsed to time, out loud
- Slide 7 names the weakest part of my own plan
:::

## After the capstone

Turn it into a case study using template 30, label it as a course project, and
put it in your portfolio. That is what the career roadmap means by "evidence",
and it is the whole reason the capstone is worth doing properly.
